description: Early blight is a common fungal disease of tomatoes caused by Alternaria solani. It primarily affects leaves, stems, and fruit.
general_management: Prune lower leaves to improve air circulation.
Avoid overhead watering to keep foliage dry.
Remove and destroy infected plant debris at the end of the season.
prevention: Practice crop rotation (avoid planting tomatoes or related crops in the same spot for 2-3 years).
Use disease-resistant varieties if available.
Apply mulch to prevent soil-borne spores from splashing onto lower leaves.
monitoring: Check lower leaves regularly for brown spots with concentric rings.

description: Late blight is a highly destructive fungal disease caused by Phytophthora infestans. It can destroy entire plants rapidly under cool, wet conditions.
general_management: Remove and destroy infected plants immediately to prevent spread.
Do not compost infected material.
prevention: Ensure good air circulation and avoid overhead watering.
Plant resistant varieties where late blight is common.
monitoring: Inspect plants frequently during cool, wet weather for large, dark, water-soaked lesions.

description: No known disease pattern detected. The plant appears healthy based on the visual patterns analyzed.
general_management: Continue standard care practices.
Maintain adequate watering and fertilization.
prevention: Maintain good field sanitation and crop rotation to prevent future issues.
monitoring: Routinely inspect plants for early signs of pests or disease.

description: Early blight of potato is a fungal disease caused by Alternaria solani, similar to early blight on tomatoes.
general_management: Ensure adequate nutrition, especially nitrogen, to help plants resist the disease.
Remove infected debris after harvest.
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed potatoes.
Rotate crops away from the nightshade family.
monitoring: Look for dark, target-like spots on older leaves.

description: Late blight is a severe disease of potatoes caused by Phytophthora infestans.
general_management: Infected plants should be removed and destroyed.
Harvest tubers only after vines are completely dead to prevent tuber infection.
prevention: Plant certified seed and use resistant varieties.
Ensure proper hilling to protect tubers.
monitoring: Watch for rapidly spreading dark lesions on leaves and stems during wet weather.

description: No known disease pattern detected. The plant appears healthy.
general_management: Continue standard potato cultivation practices.
prevention: Maintain good soil health and rotation.
monitoring: Regularly check for pests like the Colorado potato beetle and signs of blight.

description: Bacterial spot is a common disease of peppers caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria.
general_management: Avoid working in the field when plants are wet to prevent spreading the bacteria.
Remove heavily infected plant parts.
prevention: Use disease-free seed and transplants.
Practice crop rotation (at least 2 years without peppers or tomatoes).
monitoring: Look for small, water-soaked spots that turn dark on leaves.

description: No known disease pattern detected. The plant appears healthy.
general_management: Continue regular care.
prevention: Maintain standard agricultural practices.
monitoring: Check routinely for aphids and signs of bacterial spot.

description: Bacterial spot on tomato is caused by Xanthomonas species. Causes small, dark, greasy spots on foliage and fruit scabs.
general_management: Avoid overhead irrigation and handle plants only when completely dry.
Apply fixed copper bactericides early in the disease cycle.
prevention: Use certified pathogen-free seeds and hot water treatment.
Maintain a 2-year rotation with non-solanaceous crops.
monitoring: Scout weekly for circular water-soaked lesions on younger leaflets.

description: Leaf mold is caused by Passalora fulva (syn. Cladosporium fulvum), thriving in humid greenhouse and high-tunnel environments.
general_management: Increase air flow and ventilation to lower relative humidity below 85%.
Prune dense canopy and remove severely diseased lower leaves.
prevention: Plant resistant cultivars with Cladosporium resistance genes (Cf genes).
Space plants generously to promote rapid foliar drying.
monitoring: Inspect undersides of older leaves for olive-green to brown velvety patches.

description: Septoria leaf spot is caused by the fungus Septoria lycopersici. Causes circular spots with gray centers and black fruiting bodies.
general_management: Remove diseased bottom leaves promptly to slow upward progression.
Apply protective fungicides (chlorothalonil or copper) upon first symptom.
prevention: Use straw or plastic mulch to block spore splashing from soil.
Control solanaceous weeds like horsenettle that harbor the fungus.
monitoring: Examine lower leaves for 1/8-inch circular spots with tiny dark pycnidia.

description: Infestation by Tetranychus urticae causes yellow stippling, bronzing of foliage, and delicate webbing across leaf clusters.
general_management: Spray foliage with insecticidal soap or horticultural neem oil.
Introduce predatory mites (e.g., Phytoseiulus persimilis) for biological control.
prevention: Avoid excessive synthetic nitrogen fertilizers that boost mite reproduction.
Mist plants or overhead irrigate during prolonged hot, dry spells.
monitoring: Check leaf undersides with a hand lens for tiny moving mites and webbing.

description: Target spot is caused by the fungal pathogen Corynespora cassiicola, forming pinpoint lesions that expand into target-like brown rings.
general_management: Prune inner foliage to accelerate canopy drying.
Apply targeted fungicides labeled for Corynespora.
prevention: Strict sanitation: disk or bury infected plant residue after harvest.
Avoid planting adjacent to older infected cucurbit or solanaceous plantings.
monitoring: Inspect mid-canopy leaves for brown lesions with yellow chlorotic halos.

description: TYLCV is a devastating geminivirus transmitted by the sweetpotato whitefly (Bemisia tabaci), causing stunted growth and cupped leaves.
general_management: Immediately rogue and incinerate symptomatic virus-infected plants.
Deploy reflective silver mulch and yellow sticky cards to deter whiteflies.
prevention: Select TYLCV-resistant hybrids with Ty resistance genes.
Install fine insect netting (50-mesh) on nursery greenhouses.
monitoring: Regularly scout shoot tips for upward leaf curling and interveinal chlorosis.

description: ToMV is a highly stable tobamovirus causing light and dark green mottled patterns, blistering, and distorted foliage.
general_management: Disinfect pruning tools with 20% nonfat dry milk or 10% bleach solution.
Wash hands thoroughly before handling plants, especially after using tobacco.
prevention: Plant certified virus-free seed or heat-treated seed.
Choose varieties bred with Tm-2 resistance alleles.
monitoring: Scout for mosaic foliar patterns, fern-like distorted leaves, and stunted stems.
